title: Postholes reveal a possible ceremonial hall beside 5,000-year-old royal tombs
dek: Three timber buildings reconstructed from 120 postholes may have formed a ritual precinct alongside elite burials at Fanshan.
body: Archaeologists working east of the Fanshan cemetery at the Liangzhu site in Zhejiang Province have grouped 120 postholes into three timber structures that once stood beside the richest graves of the late Neolithic period. The largest, designated F1, measures about 25.2 metres by 16 metres and covers roughly 316 square metres. Its oval plan, elevated wooden floor, surrounding corridor and a roof that may have risen to 15 metres make it the most imposing building of its kind yet recognised at Liangzhu.

A second structure is circular and spans about 105 square metres. The third is roughly square and only 23 square metres. Researchers from the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology used the size and distribution of the postholes together with architectural depictions on Liangzhu pottery to produce digital reconstructions. A possible passage linking the oval and circular buildings suggests they functioned as a unit rather than in isolation.

The buildings sit directly beside Tomb M12 and other elite burials that yielded extraordinary jade cong, ceremonial axes and other prestige goods when excavated in 1986. Those objects required immense labour and technical skill, and their concentration in a few graves has long been taken as evidence of steep social hierarchy. The new structures shift attention from what was buried to what took place above ground.

Wang Ningyuan, a senior researcher at Liangzhu, proposes that the large oval building served as a xiangdian, a hall for ceremonies commemorating deceased rulers or ancestors. Its scale, unusual design and prominent position beside the cemetery make a ritual interpretation plausible. If correct, the complex would show that architecture, landscape and ceremony were integrated into a single planned precinct around 5,000 years ago.

A rectangular enclosure measuring roughly 180 by 140 metres surrounds the burial zone. Radiocarbon dates from its eastern and southern walls place construction at about 5,000 years ago, broadly matching the period of the richest tombs. That coincidence raises the possibility that walls, tombs and buildings were conceived together as a formal funerary complex rather than accumulating piecemeal.

The Liangzhu civilisation flourished in the lower Yangtze region and is noted for large settlements, water-management systems and highly specialised jade production. Until now, Fanshan has been studied mainly as a cemetery. The reconstructed buildings invite a different view: a stage for gatherings where architecture itself may have reinforced elite authority by tying living rulers to revered ancestors.

Archaeologists stress the interpretation remains provisional. No hearths, food remains, household rubbish or other traces of daily life have yet been reported from the structures. Such evidence could show that some buildings served residential rather than exclusively ceremonial purposes. Further excavation will test whether F1 was a true ritual hall or something else entirely.
doesnt_show: The postholes alone cannot confirm the buildings' function; no hearths, refuse or other occupational debris have been reported that would distinguish ritual use from residential or administrative use.
settle: Targeted excavation inside the posthole patterns for floor deposits, hearths, ritual paraphernalia or domestic waste would clarify whether F1 served as a ceremonial hall.
